faq.q: Why does shallow water slow a wave?
faq.a: Under a wave, water moves in circles. In shallow water those circles scrape along the seabed, and friction slows the bottom of the wave while the top keeps going.
asks: Why do waves get taller near the beach?

faq.q: What are the types of breaking waves?
faq.a: On gently sloping beaches, waves crumble slowly as spilling breakers. On steeper beaches they curl into tubes called plunging breakers, and on very steep shores they surge up without fully breaking.
Swash is the rush of water up the beach after a wave breaks. Backwash is the water sliding back down the slope into the sea.
asks: Why does water run back down the beach?

faq.q: Why do waves come in parallel to the beach?
faq.a: When a wave approaches at an angle, the part in shallower water slows first, so the wave swings round to line up with the shore. This bending is called refraction.
asks: Why do waves bend towards the shore?

faq.q: What makes a good surfing wave?
faq.a: The shape of the seabed controls how waves break. Reefs, sandbars and gentle points make waves peel along steadily, giving long rides.
asks: Why do surfers like certain beaches?

facts: A wave starts to feel the seabed when the water is shallower than about half its wavelength.
Waves usually break when their height reaches roughly three quarters of the water depth.

quiz.why: Friction with the shallow seabed slows the bottom of the wave, so the crest runs ahead and falls over.

wrong.1: Waves break even on calm days with no wind; it is the shallow seabed that does it.
wrong.2: The sand slows the wave by friction rather than pushing it up.
